Emigrating to America at seventeen, he won work on the Boston Pilot after a speech on repealing the Union, and O'Connell praised his early writing. Back in Dublin he joined the Young Ireland paper Nation, served as secretary of the Irish Confederation, and fled to America disguised as a priest after the rising of 1848.

In Canada he changed course entirely, entering Parliament and pressing for British supremacy as warmly as he had once pressed for revolution. Confederation owed much to his drive, and his attacks on Fenian groups made him hated by former allies. His poems and histories, including a History of Ireland in 1862, kept his literary name alive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trincomalee:
A diocese in Ceylon, suffragan of Colombo, created in 1893 by dividing the diocese of Jaffna. It covers the whole eastern province and the district of Tamankuduwa, and out of 186,251 people counts 8,773 Catholics, with 28 churches and chapels served by Jesuit fathers and two missionaries Apostolic.

Candidates for the priesthood are sent to the Kandy seminary, and the diocese runs fifty-five schools with 2,523 pupils. A convent of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Cluny, with five sisters, conducts an orphanage, and the bishop, Charles Lavigne, a Jesuit consecrated in 1887, resides at Trincomalee.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-j-har:
William J. Hardee was an American soldier and convert who wrote the army's rifle tactics manual. Born at Savannah, Georgia, in 1817, he died at Wytheville, Virginia, in 1873. He graduated from West Point in 1838, served with the second dragoons in the Florida Indian war, and in 1839 trained at the French school of Saint Maur with the French cavalry. Back in America he served in the West and rose to dragoon captain in September 1844.

Hardee fought with distinction in the Mexican War, then prepared a tactics manual finished in 1856 and became commandant of cadets at West Point. His United States Rifle and Light Infantry Tactics of 1856 borrowed chiefly from French sources rather than breaking new ground. When civil war came he joined the Confederacy, rising to lieutenant-general and corps commander, and after the war retired to his Alabama plantation.
code-three:
Code Three, by Rick Raphael, is a science fiction story of the highway patrol of tomorrow. Its head note sets the premise: cars on high-speed thruways must follow each other like sheep, and they need shepherds. The cruiser of tomorrow, it warns, must differ as much as the highways themselves.

Patrol Sergeant Ben Martin and his junior partner, Trooper Clay Ferguson, a tall Canadian, staff the Philadelphia Barracks of the North American Continental Thruway Patrol. Snow threatens as they load their car. That car, Beulah, carries magnalocks and warning lights for pinning disabled vehicles. A roadside stop shows the pair's work: secure the crippled car, light the scene, and keep the thruway moving.
coffee-and-repartee:
Coffee and Repartee, by John Kendrick Bangs, copyrighted by Harper & Brothers in 1893, is a book of comic dialogue sketches. A boarding house table supplies the stage. Its talkers carry type names: the Idiot, the School-master, and the Bibliomaniac trade remarks over coffee.

An illustration list shows the tone: Are you related to Governor McKinley? serves as frontispiece, and What are the first symptoms of insanity? heads a later page. In one sketch the Idiot returns pale from reading a book on the pleasures of country life. Country blessedness, set against the urban life the group lives, makes him feel his youth is being thrown away. The Bibliomaniac's cure is blunt: move.
doe-osti-3003211-support-for-the-32-sup-: A brief DOE award summary, for award SC0025920, closes out conference support funding. Project director Lisa A. Fredin of Lehigh University reports that the award offset registration and travel costs for the 32nd annual meeting of the Inter-American Photochemical Society. The meeting ran January 2 to 5, 2025, in Miramar Beach, Florida. Travel awards went to three assistant professors, fourteen graduate students, and two undergraduates. The summary notes the meeting's photochemistry program aligns with the Energy Department's solar photochemistry work.
doe-osti-3015204-support-for-the-30-sup-: Support for the 30th Inter-American Photochemical Society meeting is documented in a Florida State University report under award DE-SC0023655, submitted March 19, 2026, with Kenneth Hanson as principal investigator. The hosted text is chiefly the meeting program: the conference ran January 4 to 7, 2023 at the Hilton Sandestin Resort in Miramar Beach, Florida. Listings name talks on ruthenium phthalocyanines, cucurbituril host-guest chemistry, photoredox, and singlet fission, plus the 2023 Gerhard Closs lecture and poster awards. As a program record, it documents who spoke and on what, not findings.
doe-osti-3015642-integrated-direct-air-c:
A multi-lab final report under award DE-SC0022273, submitted February 2, 2026, pursues pulling carbon dioxide from air and converting it without hydrogen gas. Hongfei Lin led the work. Partners sat at four national laboratories and Vanderbilt. The consortium ran from September 2021 to August 2025.

Five direct air capture sorbent systems were built. They include calcium oxide and superbase ionic liquid composites, and nickel MOF ionic liquid hybrids. Capacities reached up to 1.86 millimoles per gram at 400 parts per million, with strong cycling stability. For conversion, a zinc-oxygen-chromium catalyst on SSZ-13 zeolite co-converted ethane and carbon dioxide. The run temperature was 500 degrees Celsius. It gave about 9.6 percent ethane conversion at full ethylene selectivity. Carbon dioxide utilization hit 99.0 percent.
doe-osti-3028321-final-report-for-closin:
Y Lu, K Kroll, A Bunger, M Cusini, F Fei, and C Wang of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, with the University of Utah as award recipient. They close a project on enhanced geothermal systems in LLNL-TR-2017584, dated April 2026. Its title states the loop to close: underground stress is complex, the fractures made for geothermal heat mining are complex, and the two should explain each other. If fracture shapes reveal stress, operators can read a reservoir before they finish building it.

Simulations sort fracture alignment into two families, fractures running along the well and fractures inclined to it. In a vertical well, inclined fractures appear when the wellbore deviates relative to the maximum horizontal stress direction. A further idea measures the curvature of the near-well fracture and ties it to deviation angle and stress size, which the authors offer as a more robust stress analysis tool.
doe-osti-3030823-supporting-resource-ade:
Prateek Joshi presents this slide set, dated September 2025, on the ReEDS-India model and how it guards resource adequacy, the ability of a power system to meet demand. ReEDS-India is an open-access planning tool from the National Laboratory of the Rockies. It picks the lowest-cost mix of generation, transmission, and storage for India mid- and long-term needs. Each state and union territory forms one balancing area, 34 in all, and wind and solar draw on 147 resource regions.

Slides cover how weather data, planning reserves, and time scales enter the model. Runs span 2025 to 2070, solved in five-year steps. A default planning reserve takes 5 percent of national demand in each time slice, open to adjustment. Gas, diesel, hydro, coal, nuclear, storage, biomass, and hydrogen turbines can all supply reserves.
domestic-cookery-useful-receipts-and-hin:
Elizabeth E. Lea wrote her cookery book for young women facing a first household with little training. The hosted text is the third edition, much revised, with new matter under the hints and mixed receipts. Lea says she gathered the directions from skilled housekeepers and from her own trials, since books of the day served grand dishes and skipped plain ones.

Receipts cover meats and poultry, sauces, pickles, and preserves, with exact measures in spoons, cups, and pounds. A spiced sauce, for one, takes mustard seed, cloves, pepper, onion, and salt, and keeps under a layer of spirits. Hints to young housekeepers teach order, thrift, and care of stores. The book treats plain cooking as skilled work, and it gives a new mistress the steps to do it well from her first week.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DiesCommittee_D: nsia-DiesCommittee Dies Committee: the made public government document on the Dies Committee, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DiesSubcommitte:
On June 22, 1944, members of the U.S. House of Representatives debated the work of the Dies Committee on the House floor. An excerpt from the Congressional Record preserves that discussion. The committee, chaired by Martin Dies, was then investigating alleged un-American activity inside the United States.

Floor debates show a committee fighting for its standing in real time. Supporters and critics spoke for the record while the panel's funding and methods were contested in Congress itself. For readers, the excerpt is a direct sample of how the Dies Committee was argued about by the lawmakers who created it.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ParmanWalterLee: Walter Lee Parman is named in the title of this declassified US government document, archived by the Internet Archive. The record carries no year, no issuing body, no abstract. Public text not found. It waits here as a name and a file number.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_intellig: The Pike Committee was the House of Representatives' 1975 investigation into American intelligence, the partner to the Senate's Church Committee. Its clashes with the Ford White House over access and publication became a story in themselves. This briefing-book page presents the record of that three-way fight among the White House, the CIA, and the committee. The evidence here is the title alone. The subject still matters, because the Pike fight set lasting precedents for how much Congress may see of secret operations.
immensee:
Theodor Storm's Immensee is a short German tale, here translated by C. W. Bell, about memory, youth and a love that time has altered. The edition belongs to a series meant to help English readers meet foreign literature without a bulky dictionary, pairing literary worth with useful vocabulary.

Storm tells his story in the quiet, reflective manner that made his name, letting an older man's return to familiar places stir the scenes of his youth. The lake and woods of the title give the tale its still centre, and Bell's translation aims to join readable English style with strict faithfulness to Storm's German. Readers new to German fiction will find Immensee a gentle, brief introduction to one of its most loved storytellers.
in-the-year-of-jubilee:
George Gissing opens In the Year of Jubilee on a Sunday morning in Camberwell, a respectable suburb of London. Arthur Peachey slips away for his first holiday since his marriage. His wife Ada keeps a showy, slovenly house in De Crespigny Park. Her friends the French sisters, sharp Beatrice and flighty Fanny, fill the rooms with talk.

Gissing follows these young women as they chafe against dull homes and narrow prospects. Courtships, advertisements, and schemes for advancement drive the plot forward. The jubilee year of Queen Victoria gives the book its backdrop of public cheer. Beneath the comedy runs a hard look at marriage, money, and female ambition. Few Victorian novelists watched suburban life with a colder or funnier eye than Gissing shows here.
jack-harkaway-and-his-son-s-escape-from-:
Bracebridge Hemyng's Jack Harkaway and His Son's Escape from the Brigands of Greece continues the Harkaways' Greek adventures. The book opens with a scolding: Mrs. Harkaway's maid, long on an errand, returns with twenty excuses, none of them true.

She has been detained by the Contessa Maraviglia, whose letter invites the Harkaways to a grand ball at the Palazzo Maraviglia. Midnight marauders, house-breaking, a mendicant friar and the brigands of the title soon follow. Hemyng writes rattling boys' adventure, and readers who enjoy Victorian tales of Greece, brigands and daring escapes will find this volume full of incident.
literary-character-of-men-of-genius-draw:
Isaac Disraeli draws these studies from writers' own confessions. His son, the Earl of Beaconsfield, edited this new edition. Frederick Warne published it in London in 1850. Disraeli's preface promises unity across his vernacular literature writings.

The pieces initiate readers into England's national literature, he claims. They also open a comprehensive view of human nature. Authors' faculties, tastes, fortunes, and feelings supply the evidence. Genius appears here through its own words rather than gossip. Gradations of faculties shape the portraits across the volume. Thinking materials, not literary topics alone, justify his collection.
murder-in-any-degree:
Owen Johnson gathers nine stories in this 1913 Century volume. Johnson had won fame with Stover at Yale and The Varmint. Two artists drew the pictures for the book. The title tale, Murder in Any Degree, leads the set.

Other tales include One Hundred in the Dark and A Comedy for Wives. The Lie, Even Threes, and Larry Moore fill out the list. Wedding gifts and a lottery bring lighter plots. Johnson writes of school, college, and married life with a shrewd eye. The set shows his range, from campus humor to darker tales of choice and chance.
nasa-tm-19710011740-a-specialized-model-:
S S Manson and C R Ensign of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a spring 1971 structures meeting in London. It offers a model for studying creep rupture data. Creep rupture is the slow failure of hot metal under steady load. Engineers need sound ways to stretch short test results into long service life forecasts.

Many rival time and heat formulas existed, with no agreed way to pick the best one. Manson's approach sidesteps that choice. Its general relation can contain all the common formulas at once. Each formula gets an equal chance to prove itself. The model defines its curves by values at chosen stations, not by fixed math forms.
north-of-fifty-three:
Bertrand W. Sinclair published North of Fifty-Three with Little, Brown in 1914, and Grosset and Dunlap reissued it in New York. Anton Otto Fischer drew the pictures. The frontispiece shows a woman gasping at gold. Sinclair had written The Land of Frozen Suns before this tale.

Chapter one introduces a lady and two gentlemen, the contents promise. Heart, hand, and pocketbook, then a will's bequest, stir the plot. Cariboo Meadows brings the northern gold country into view. A different sort of man, deep water, and the house that Jack built follow. Winter and a truce, the fires of spring, and the out trail close the listed chapters.
on-the-trail-of-grant-and-lee:
Frederick Trevor Hill wrote this joint study of Grant and Lee. The foreword recalls a taunt put to Minister Charles Adams. Adams replied that Confederate victories were won by fellow countrymen. Nearly fifty years had passed since that exchange, Hill notes. Local pride had twisted the Civil War story, he argues.

Hill urges North and South to share pride in American courage. Lincoln is now a national heritage, not a local hero, he says. Grant and Lee differed in views, tastes, and sympathies. Each still showed qualities that should make Americans proud. Hill places neither man on a pedestal. Their trials are followed as a very human story.
podcast-joerogan-0-Jalhl4CEE:
Andrew Wilson joins Joe Rogan for episode 2444 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Wilson is a debater known for sharp clashes on faith, morals, and the culture wars. His visits to big shows tend to spark heat.

Wilson and Rogan spar over the grounds of right and wrong and the place of God in them. Wilson holds a hard line and loves a clean win on points. Rogan tests him with the doubts his crowd sends in. Listeners who love a frank debate get one here at full length. The library keeps the episode as a record of the clash.
podcast-tuckercarlson-eRlkcRnC9eE:
Billionaire investor Chamath Palihapitiya joins Tucker Carlson to talk tech titans and a promised golden age under Trump. Chamath, a former Facebook leader turned venture capitalist, co-hosts the All-In podcast. He gives an insider's view of Zuckerberg, Rogan, and Musk and their place in the new order.

The two discuss how Silicon Valley's leaders shifted toward Trump and why. Chamath lays out his case that looser rules and new energy policy could spark a boom. Carlson tests the optimism against the fears of workers left behind before. Curious viewers get a rich insider's map of tech and power.
prisoners-of-chance-the-story-of-what-be:
Randall Parrish published a frontier romance with A. C. McClurg of Chicago in 1908, telling what befell Geoffrey Benteen, a borderman, through his love for a lady of France. Colour pictures by the Kinneys illustrate the book.

Opening chapters carry a request for aid, a risky venture, and a visit to a flag-ship, placing the hero between wilderness fighting and French colonial power. Parrish, known for tales of the old West and border wars, mixes battle, travel, and courtship. Readers get a fast story of loyalty and danger on an early American frontier.
recollections-and-letters-of-general-rob:
Captain Robert E. Lee, the general's son, wrote this life of his father from family memory and the general's own letters. Early chapters cover the elder Lee's service in the United States Army, his return from the Mexican War, and his years as head of West Point. He also helped suppress the John Brown raid at Harper's Ferry.

War chapters follow his choice to resign and lead the Virginia forces, his counsel to President Davis, and command of the Army of Northern Virginia. Letters to his wife and daughters run through accounts of Chancellorsville, Gettysburg, and the winter of 1863-4. The contents end with Cold Harbour and the siege of Petersburg.
scientific-american-volume-xxxvi-no-8-fe: Scientific American for February 24, 1877, is Volume XXXVI, Number 8, new series, priced at three dollars and twenty cents per annum with postage prepaid. Munn and Company, at Number 37 Park Row in New York, edit and own the weekly, founded in 1845; O. D. Munn and A. E. Beach are named on the masthead. Facing matter explains that the Supplement is a distinct paper, issued weekly with sixteen octavo pages and a handsome cover. Its own subscription runs five dollars a year, and single copies sell for ten cents.
soldiers-three: Rudyard Kipling heads a set of tales Soldiers Three, dated 1895, joined on the title page with The Story of the Gadsbys and In Black and White. The contents name The God from the Machine, Of Those Called, and Private Learoyd's Story. Later tales cover the Big Drunk Draf', the wreck of the Visigoth, the Solid Muldoon, and With the Main Guard. The first tale opens under a maxim of Private Mulvaney: hit a man and help a woman, and you cannot be far wrong.
stingaree:
E. W. Hornung wrote Stingaree, first copyrighted in 1905 and printed by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York in 1910, with pictures by George W. Lambert. The book collects linked tales of an Australian bushranger who announces himself with the cry that gives him his name.

The opening chapters move from a voice in the wilderness to the black hole of Glenranald, then to a bushranger at bay. Hornung was known for tales of daring rogues. He sets the action in the bush country of Australia. There Stingaree's escapes, disguises, and cool manners turn crime stories into adventure. The touch stays light and wry throughout.
stories-of-inventors-the-adventures-of-i:
Russell Doubleday's Stories of Inventors, dated 1904, bears the subtitle The Adventures of Inventors and Engineers and promises true incidents and personal experiences. A frontispiece shows Marconi reading a message, setting the book's up-to-date tone.

The contents explain how Marconi telegraphs without wires, how Santos-Dumont flies his air-ship, how a fast train is run, and how automobiles work. Other chapters ride the fastest steamboats, visit life-savers and bridge builders, and look at submarines, long-distance telephony, moving pictures, a thinking typesetting machine, and making ice by heat. It is a tour of new machines told through the men who ran them.
story-hour-readers-book-three:
Ida Coe, an assistant principal in the New York City public schools, and Alice J. Christie, a primary teacher in the same system, prepared Story Hour Readers, Book Three, for the third year. It is a school reader built wholly from stories, poems, myths, and fables.

The contents open with Stevenson's The Land of Story Books. Hansel and Gretel and Longfellow's Hiawatha pieces follow. Then comes a run of Indian folklore. It holds The Beavers' Lodge, Manitou and the Squirrels, and Brother Rabbit. Greek tales of Diana and Apollo, Aesop's fables, northern folklore, and a Japanese hermit tale broaden the set. Short pieces and frequent changes keep young readers moving.
the-absentee: Maria Edgeworth wrote The Absentee, a novel. Its contents list a set of notes on the tale. Chapters numbered one through thirteen and beyond then follow. No chapter titles are given. The front notes explain two marks in the text. Notes from the print book sit in square brackets. The pound sign is written as the letter L.
the-apricot-tree:
A short tale for the Society for Promoting Christian Knowledge, printed in London in 1851 and sold for twopence, opens on a fine autumn evening. The last sun rays fall through the window of a cottage standing in a pleasant lane a quarter mile from the village of Ryefield.

A narrow gravel walk leads to the cottage door between two small plots. On the right grow cabbages, onions, and other useful greens. On the left stand gooseberry and currant bushes, with one strip of flowers: stocks, sweet-peas, and rose-trees in full bloom over a neat quick-hedge. The neat, well-kept garden sets the scene for the moral tale the title promises.
the-bullitt-mission-to-russia-testimony-: The Bullitt Mission to Russia holds the testimony of William C. Bullitt before the Committee on Foreign Relations of the United States Senate, dated 1919. The list of heads starts with the committee meeting and Bullitt's official status. Ordered to Russia, the Council of Ten discussing Russia, and the troops at Archangel come next. What America wanted, the British terms, and the text of a projected peace proposal follow. Bullitt's report on Russia fills the next block, on its economic, social, and political state, with peace proposals and conclusions.
the-chief-legatee: Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, wrote this mystery, copyrighted in 1906 and shown here in a special Weinstock, Lubin and Co. edition with water-color pictures by Frank T. Merrill. Only the front matter and the start of the contents are present here. Part I is headed A Woman of Mystery, and its chapters open with a bride of five hours and a lady in number three.Nothing inside the book follows its front matter.
the-conflict-with-slavery-part-1-from-th: John Greenleaf Whittier's prose on slavery fills this volume, whose contents page runs from early pieces like Justice and Expediency and The Abolitionists. Later items treat Kansas, William Lloyd Garrison, and the election of 1872. Later sections turn to reform and politics, woman suffrage, Italian unity, and aid for the blind. Only the title page and contents are present here, so the essays themselves do not appear.
the-fruit-of-the-tree:
Edith Wharton wrote The Fruit of the Tree as a novel of mills and morals, printed at New York in 1907 with pictures by Alonzo Kimball. A hurt mill hand stands at the start.

In the surgical ward of Hope Hospital at Hanaford, a nurse bends over a young man whose right hand and arm lie bound in bandages. He asks if there is any show for him, meaning a chance to work again. Wharton sets a nurse's care, a mill owner's wealth, and a wife's cold rule in one frame, and asks what the rich owe to the folk their mills maim.
the-holly-tree:
The Holly-Tree, in three branches, is shown transcribed from the 1894 Chapman and Hall edition of Christmas Stories. No author is named in the pages present. The first branch, Myself, opens with a confession: the narrator has kept one secret in his life, and the secret is that he is a bashful man by nature.

That shyness, he says, explains countless places not visited and calls not made. His object is a plain account of being snowed up at the Holly-Tree Inn, a house of good entertainment for man and beast. The journey began in grief, after he parted forever from Angela Leath, who preferred his bosom friend Edwin, and resolved to sail for America.
the-life-of-the-bee:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote his famous essays on bees, and Alfred Sutro translated them for a New York edition of 1914, first published in May 1901. Contents run from the threshold of the hive through the swarm, young queens, the nuptial flight, and the massacre of the males. Chapter one opens with a disclaimer.

Maeterlinck says he offers no manual of bee keeping and no strict science monograph on bee species. Fine manuals already exist in France, England, and Germany, he notes. His book follows hive life as a drama of work, birth, flight, and death inside one small city.
the-portygee:
Joseph Crosby Lincoln's The Portygee opens on a raw December night at the South Harniss railway station. Clouds cloak the sky, pines thresh on the hilltops, and a wet, salty wind off the sea tears over dunes and frozen salt-meadows. It screams through the telegraph wires. The platform, in the narrator's judgment, is the lonesomest and most miserable spot imaginable: cold, dark, and forsaken.

At least, that is the opinion of the seventeen-year-old boy the down train has just deposited there, on time for once. Three other men share the platform: the station agent, Jim Young, who drives the depot wagon and whistles Silver Bells, and Doctor Holliday, the homeopath. Holliday is home from Boston and puffing a cigar. The boy looks out at black earth and sky beyond the station's kerosene gleam. He finds even the train's smelly warmth luxurious by comparison.
the-tale-of-buster-bumblebee: Arthur Scott Bailey's Slumber-Town tale of Buster Bumblebee was published by Grosset and Dunlap in 1918, illustrated by Harry L. Smith. Only the title pages and publisher's lists are present in this record, placing the book among Bailey's Tuck-Me-In tales alongside Jolly Robin, Old Mr. Crow and Solomon Owl, Jasper Jay and Rusty Wren, and Daddy Longlegs and Kiddie Katydid, so Buster's own adventures do not appear.
the-world-set-free:
H. G. Wells wrote The World Set Free in 1913 and published it early in 1914. His preface calls it the latest of three fantasias of possibility. Each story imagines future developments of some contemporary force. Wells dedicates the book to Frederick Soddy's Interpretation of Radium. Long passages, he admits, owe much to that work's eleventh chapter. Chapters promise a new source of energy and a last war.

Wells says the story was written under the Great War's immediate shadow. Intelligent people everywhere felt disaster approaching in 1914. Few realized how near the crash already was. The novel famously imagines atomic bombs decades early. Its preface shows Wells thinking aloud about science and catastrophe.
